# Data Preparation

This analysis examines the reliability and construct validity of two multi-item scales in Case 31:

-   R3: Attitude toward Employee Proficiency (Q3–Q6)
-   R6: Attitude toward Operational Effectiveness (Q31–Q34)

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false

library(haven)
library(dplyr)
library(psych)
library(ggplot2)
library(knitr)

efcu <- read_sav("../Case 31 Data_efcu_4.sav")
names(efcu) <- tolower(names(efcu))
```

## Variable Selection

```{r}
r3_items <- efcu |>
  select(q3, q4, q5, q6)

r6_items <- efcu |>
  select(q31, q32, q33, q34)

dim(efcu)

summary(r3_items)
summary(r6_items)
```

# R3: Attitude toward Employee Proficiency

## Exploratory Factor Analysis

Exploratory factor analysis is conducted on Q3–Q6
to examine whether the four items measure a single
underlying construct.

### KMO and Bartlett's Test

```{r}
psych::KMO(r3_items)

psych::cortest.bartlett(
  cor(r3_items),
  n = nrow(r3_items)
)
```

### Parallel Analysis

```{r}
#| label: fig-r3-parallel
#| fig-cap: "Parallel Analysis for Employee Proficiency"
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 5

set.seed(123)

psych::fa.parallel(
  r3_items,
  fa = "fa",
  fm = "minres",
  n.iter = 100
)
```

### Factor Loadings and Communalities

```{r}
r3_efa <- psych::fa(
  r3_items,
  nfactors = 1,
  rotate = "none",
  fm = "minres"
)

print(r3_efa, digits = 3)
```

### Interpretation

The KMO value of 0.78 and significant Bartlett's
test (p < 0.001) indicate that the data are
suitable for factor analysis.

Factor loadings range from 0.722 to 0.923, and
all communalities exceed 0.50. The one-factor
solution explains 63.3% of the total variance,
providing evidence of convergent validity.

However, the model fit indices suggest that the
one-factor structure should be interpreted with
caution. Further reliability and discriminant
validity analyses are needed before confirming
the composite scale.

# R6: Attitude toward Operational Effectiveness

## Exploratory Factor Analysis

Exploratory factor analysis is conducted on Q31–Q34
to assess the convergent validity of the operational
effectiveness scale.

### KMO and Bartlett's Test

```{r}
psych::KMO(r6_items)

psych::cortest.bartlett(
  cor(r6_items),
  n = nrow(r6_items)
)
```

### Parallel Analysis

```{r}
#| label: fig-r6-parallel
#| fig-cap: "Parallel Analysis for Operational Effectiveness"
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 5

set.seed(123)

r6_parallel <- psych::fa.parallel(
  r6_items,
  fa = "fa",
  fm = "minres",
  n.iter = 100
)

r6_parallel$nfact
```

### Factor Loadings and Communalities

```{r}
r6_efa <- psych::fa(
  r6_items,
  nfactors = 1,
  rotate = "none",
  fm = "minres"
)

print(r6_efa, digits = 3)
```

### Interpretation

The KMO value of 0.50 indicates marginal sampling
adequacy. Although Bartlett's test is significant
(p < 0.001), most factor loadings and communalities
are low.

The one-factor solution explains only 31.4% of
the variance and produces an ultra-Heywood case.
These results indicate weak convergent validity
and do not support creating a composite scale
at this stage.

# Combined Factor Analysis

## Discriminant Validity

A combined factor analysis is conducted on Q3–Q6
and Q31–Q34 to examine whether employee proficiency
and operational effectiveness represent two
distinct constructs.

### Parallel Analysis

```{r}
combined_items <- cbind(r3_items, r6_items)
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-combined-parallel
#| fig-cap: "Parallel Analysis for Both Constructs"
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 5

set.seed(123)

combined_parallel <- psych::fa.parallel(
  combined_items,
  fa = "fa",
  fm = "minres",
  n.iter = 100
)

combined_parallel$nfact
```

### Two-Factor Solution

```{r}
combined_efa <- psych::fa(
  combined_items,
  nfactors = 2,
  rotate = "oblimin",
  fm = "minres"
)

print(combined_efa, digits = 3, cutoff = 0)

combined_efa$Phi
```

### Factor Diagram

```{r}
#| label: fig-combined-factor
#| fig-cap: "Factor Structure of R3 and R6"
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 6

psych::fa.diagram(combined_efa)
```

### Interpretation

Parallel analysis suggests a two-factor structure.
R3 items load strongly on the same factor, while
R6 items show weak and inconsistent loadings.

The factor correlation is 0.401. However, the
ultra-Heywood case and weak R6 loadings indicate
that discriminant validity is not fully supported.

# Reliability Analysis

Cronbach's alpha is used to assess the internal
consistency of the R3 and R6 multi-item scales.

## R3: Employee Proficiency

```{r}
r3_alpha <- psych::alpha(r3_items)

print(r3_alpha, digits = 3)
```

## R6: Operational Effectiveness

```{r}
r6_alpha <- psych::alpha(r6_items)

print(r6_alpha, digits = 3)
```

## Reliability Summary

```{r}
reliability_summary <- data.frame(
  Scale = c("R3", "R6"),
  Items = c(4, 4),
  Cronbach_Alpha = c(
    r3_alpha$total$raw_alpha,
    r6_alpha$total$raw_alpha
  )
)

knitr::kable(
  reliability_summary,
  digits = 3,
  caption = "Reliability Analysis Summary"
)
```

## Interpretation

R3 demonstrates good internal consistency
(Cronbach's alpha = 0.866). Removing any item
reduces reliability, supporting the retention
of all four items.

R6 demonstrates low internal consistency
(Cronbach's alpha = 0.472). Removing individual
items does not substantially improve reliability.
Therefore, the R6 items should be analyzed
individually.

# Composite Scale Decision and Conclusion

## R3: Employee Proficiency

R3 demonstrates good internal consistency
(alpha = 0.866) and strong factor loadings.
Despite limitations in model fit, Q3–Q6 can
be combined into a composite scale by averaging
the four items, with caution.

## R6: Operational Effectiveness

R6 demonstrates low reliability (alpha = 0.472)
and weak convergent validity. Therefore, Q31–Q34
should be analyzed individually rather than
combined into a composite scale.

## Conclusion

The results support using a composite scale for
R3 with caution, but not for R6. Discriminant
validity is only partially supported.
